title: What part of game making do you find most difficult?

posts.author: Garryg
posts.body:
What order would you put the following development activities in?
Mine are as follows. 1 being most difficult...
1) Coming up with the Story-line and Plot.
2) Making the graphics.
3) Creating Music and Sound effects.
4) Writing the dialogue.
5) Programming/Scripting effects.
I've worked as a profesional developer for over ten years in the past and have an interest in creative writing, with a few short stories being published in print and on line. So the programming aspects arn't really that much of an issue and I'm ok at dialogue. I'm not much of an artist though and my music skills are 'limited' to say the least.
But coming up with a coherent story, far less a good one, has always been by far the hardest part for me. Not so important when I'm making arcade games for the ATARI 2600, Vectrex, or VIC20 etc. but defenetly the hardest part when the game-play requires it as a fundamental part of the design like in RPG type games..
I'd be interested in hearing about other peoples lists and background.

posts.author: Piyan Glupak
posts.body:
Hardest aspect for me is the detailed story line and plot. I get plenty of overall ideas, but I tend to stall when I need to think of intermediate or side quests.
Second hardest is writing plugins. I am not very comfortable with JavaScript, and often have difficulty working out exactly what the main .js files of RPG Maker are actually doing at any particular point. It takes me a lot longer to produce a small plugin than it would for many people, and I have to be in a specific mood to even want to start.

posts.author: Robro33
posts.body:
the art is definitely the biggest hurdle for me. I enjoy making my own music, story, and scripting. admittedly, I still need to work on my dialogue as to not have everyone sound like the same person, but i like writing out conversations between characters and ive intentionally left it to do later in development as i work on other things. Whenever i sit down and go "i want to learn to draw this thing", its usually an hour or two of me accomplishing nothing and moving on to something else I enjoy doing.
I thought mapping sucked until i got MZ and started using it for for the layer control. I do limited mapping since I know at some point ill be changing the tilesets around, but using MZ for it made it so much better
The thing thats taken the most time for me is drafting and scripting the mechanics alongside testing. I started with the mechanics first because its something I could immediately work on without much need to change later. I also just really enjoy making mechanics and gimmicks for gear/characters/classes/bosses and physically cannot stop myself. Balance is kinda up in the air till i finish a few planned systems.

posts.author: Prescott
posts.body:
Getting people to play. Most of the people that worked on the game with me haven't even played it yet lol.
Actually though, the hardest part for me is combat and combat balance. I don't want to say I have no idea what I'm doing, but man it's a really hard part for me. There is a reason why practically none of the little games I have made in the past have combat in them. I usually opt for horror games, or adventure games, stuff where if there is combat it's extremely simple. Now that I'm making a full-blown RPG, the combat needs to be there and it's been pretty hard for me.
Dungeon design is also not my strong suite. I'm really bad at developing puzzles. I had a couple of people help me with the dungeon design.
Most everything else is pretty easy for me, now that I've been doing it for so long. It can be hard to find the motivation to work sometimes, but once I start it's pretty easy for the most part. Few hang-ups now and then of course, but thankfully I've got this community for that
The music is by far the easiest part. I made the entire soundtrack for my current game in a month or two. Still consider some of those tracks as the best ones I've ever made.
(I didn't even take art into account because I did basically none of it; it was all commissioned).

posts.author: Cythera

Hmm, for all my complaining about making maps, I don't find it difficult - just time consuming.
I'd say, for me the hardest part of game making is the visual polishing, and making animations. By visual polishing, I mean the lil extras that go a mile. Things like changing the char sprite for when they're sitting down vs standing up vs taking damage in a cutscene, etc. etc.
Making animations is very self-explanatory. Hence why I tend to just...use the ones that come pre-made in packs...
Then there's playtesting, but again. That's more time-consuming than difficult

posts.author: kaukusaki
posts.body:
Hm...
1) Coming up with the Story-line and Plot. - i have hella stories (been writing tree killers almost 30 years now). sometimes when i don't feel like thinking too hard, i roll plots unlimited/plotto and make a game based off the results. sometimes the rando weirdness helps get the brain juices flowing. i like making rando works (that has their own internal logic of course).
2 ) Making the graphics (sprites, maps, animations, UI). - using my art degree. fun times.
3) Creating Music and Sound effects. - using my sound engineering degree. fun times.
4) Writing the dialogue. - using my literary arts degree. fun times.
5) Programming/Scripting effects. - again using my tech degree. lol fun times.
Really, there isn't anything i can't do to make RM jump through hoops. it's just poor health and puter gremlins keep pushing things back. my goal was to make it more than an RDK and prove that one can make professional games with it. Been in the biz 20 years and using RM professionally for 9 of them (it'll be 10 come  June 2025 lol).
Now that I been hit with the Parkinson's dx, my memory's been shorting lately and it's getting harder to type. Now I know i have even more limited time to get these projects done.
i 've learned to reign in feature creep and mechanics bloat. and i got a good grasp on keeping to the SRD & GDD. My only worry is if the game is fun and challenging enough but not too difficult to be throwing controllers. I have fun creating it and testing it. but i'm an old head, so i'm used to difficult games.
that's the only unknown variable that makes me sweat before upload. i'm not sure what the kids are into. i been stuck between hospital and office bubble for the past 13 years.
all i can do is offer up what I know while market research team helps me stay on top what's trending, fun and cool. I just hope once i finally hit send that players like my creations. i stopped dreaming of making money off my products (since what monies i have are sunk into staying alive.)
just have fun with it kids.

posts.author: Tai_MT
posts.body:
Mostly anything "artsy" is what I have issues with.  If it's visual art, I am more or less incompetent.  I lack the brain for it.  If there ever comes a day when the things I imagine can be plastered wholesale into a medium and show up exactly as I envision, I will have no problems with art anymore.  My hands and eyes cannot do what my brain does imagine.
On the other hand, anything "system" related, I have a knack for.  Or, storytelling related.  I do not program and largely can't (I probably COULD, but I lack the patience for it, so I never bothered with it... though I have very few problems reading coding and following what it's being told to do).  I have similar issues with composing music (no patience for it, especially since I play largely by feel and learn largely by ear and can't read sheet music, much less compose anything very easily without just randomly faffing about with notes until I hear something pleasing).
I do worldbuilding exceptionally well, however.  Dialogue I do decently.  Anything to do with a "system", I do pretty well, including spotting flaws in it and putting fixes in place usually before execution.

posts.author: ISC
posts.body:
1) Making the graphics.
2) Creating Music and Sound effects.
3) Writing the dialogue.
4) Coming up with the Story-line and Plot.
5) Programming/Scripting effects.
Anyone who knows me knows that I hate mapping. I know that for many it’s a relaxing activity, but for me it’s a nightmare because with every tile they add, I tell myself that the artwork wasn’t created by me. This weakness of mine affects my game design, so I often create games with great mechanics but that are visually unappealing. This is because, for years, I’ve been more of an experimenter than an aspiring dev. I can recreate all the mechanics I think of, but when it comes to presenting them visually, I get blocked. So yes, game design and graphics are the hardest parts for me, while programming and planning are the easiest

posts.author: ElvenNeko
posts.body:
Programming is the worst, because i barely understand it in general (despite several years attempts of learning it). It just like entirely different world. Also it often requires calculations that i also can't do well.
Art is the second after programming. I have almost no visual imagination, so i can describe what i want to see to someone, but can't draw it myself because i don't exactly know how it will look like. I can do very simple edits in pixel art, like adding a tear, but something more complicated like colors of clothing is beyond me. I always try to make color gradation to make it look like real thing, but it always looks like  because i don't know which colors and where they should be. I know what i want, but don't know how to do that. Ai changed that game a lot, since instead of drawing i can just describe what i want with words, and that is like dream come true for me. And level design is also sometimes hard for the same reason.
Writing is the easiest part for me, since i adore good stories and know how they should be made, what to avoid, how to pace it, how to develop characters, etc. It all comes very naturally to me, like i always could do that. But i also can work only with very limited amount of genres - mostly sci-fi and fantasy, sometimes drama. The rest are either unknown to me, or are something i never tried before - for example, recently i tried to create a satirical parody, and not sure if i did well or not - some people found it hilarious, others - not funny at all. Maybe it depends on sense of humor and mine only appeals to certain audience, idk. But anyway it was refreshing experience to try something new. Also i was writing a lot of poetry for that project (song texts) that were also a new thing for me. Few of them went surprisingly easy, while some took weeks of changing lyrics to find perfect rhymes without losing the subject of the song. Would i do that again? Maybe, some day. But i perfer writing stories more)

posts.author: freakytapir
posts.body:
Besides giving a damn about visual art, ...
Not stampeding off and start making content before the foundations are laid, making it so I have to redo and redo and redo everything every time a new shiny plug-in catches my eye or I come back after months of inactivity.
So now, I've made myself a
promise
: I don't make any piece of non-Playtest content until everything works, and then, only then do I start actually making the game.
Every system has to work in its base form before I start making content.
Working combat system.
A Fighter (to test the taunt system), Rogue (to see if my skill system works and positionals in combat), Cleric (Healing spellcaster) and Wizard (Offensive caster).
Maybe five enemies (Melee, Ranged, Caster, Healer, Boss).
Only the necessary status effects
Just enough spells to test combat balance.
Levels 1-3.
One boxed out dungeon. A single journal entry that works and updates beginning to end.
A combat system that works 100%.
A way to mass edit, analyze and graph out my class parameters in one go. (Which I actually got to work. Jay for CVS files and Rstudio)
Making sure I have portraits finalized before writing even one dialoge box I intend to keep...
Only start making charactersi RPG Maker once I'm writing the story.
Only start adding classes once I got class balance down pat.
So basically Keep myself in check, so once I get to content generation it goes smooth. (And also have an empty project I can base my other games off of, so I don't have to redo all this).

Good characters are where it's at.

Persona 4 is very guilty of this. I mean, the main story is "guy kidnaps people and throws them into TV's because he as some messiah complex while the real culprit sits laughing from the sidelines and in the end it's all a game between some inscrutable divine beings about what Humanity 'wants'.
But I adore Yosuke. Kanji, Naoto, Chie (Yukiko can go ride the vanilla express with Haru). Even Teddy is hatable in a fun way. What you've described doesn't feel very "barebones" to me – summing up mystery stories like that is always going to make them sound silly, but it's mostly the buildup that counts in the case of this genre. But two people can feel very differently about a work, so let's agree to disagree in this.
As for the dichotomy of story-driven versus character-driven storytelling – both are good in their own ways. They have their differences, but they have a lot of overlap, too. I wouldn't say character-driven storytelling is always preferable. It mostly depends on the genre and overall feel you're going for, including how action-packed you want your game to be (character-driven stories tend to be slower). It's not always the "correct" choice to just focus on characters. Not to mention it takes quite a bit of skill to write compelling, engaging characters. It's not an easy fix.

posts.author: Tai_MT
posts.body:
As with most things, it's "use the right tool for the job".
I'm not sure this will make sense to anyone, but I'll give it a shot.
If the point of the story is the main storyline (you have a mystery to be solved), then generally the characters don't typically matter that much.  After all, the story exists for the AUDIENCE to figure it out, not for the CHARACTERS to figure it out.  There are other genre examples of this that aren't mystery, but they're usually "this is the premise, what happens as a result of the premise?" type stories.  These are stories where the events matter more than the characters.
So, you need to write a compelling "story" in those instances.
If the point of your story is "how do the characters act/react to events", then generally the main storyline matters very little in any context.  After all, the main draw would be the characters and them being likable or interesting.  Usually this is the most versatile writing option available, however, since the "main story" can be completely crap so long as everyone likes or relates to the characters (you can look at Young Adult novels as the poster child for this sort of thing.  The world of The Hunger Games makes literally zero sense, but the characters are why anyone is reading those... and the story of Twilight is pretty bad and beyond basic... but people were invested in the love story between Bella and Edward, so that basic and stupid storyline didn't matter at all).
But, there's also a third option in here.
Exploriation of an idea/concept.
Where the story AND the characters don't really matter.  The example I like to cite is "Starship Troopers" for something like this, but there are many other examples across the genre.  The reason I cite "Starship Troopers", is because it's one of my favorite books and its also very simply constructed so th at anyone reading it knows exactly what I mean by "exploring an idea".
Starship Troopers follows Johnny Rico on his way to "becoming an officer in the military".  But, we get very little about who Johnny is as a person, what he thinks, or even what he feels.  Johnny serves as our "point of reference" for the system of government he lives under as well as a mouthpiece for (presumably) the author's personal politics.  So, it's not a character driven story.  On top of which, the story itself is "Johnny enlisted in the military shortly before humanity went to war with an alien bug species, and this is how rough it's going for humanity".  Pretty basic, mostly glossed over, only slightly interesting (when the movie was made, they basically turned the war against the bugs into the primary draw, which was excellent, since the alien species had the potential to be VERY INTERESTING as a complete unknown to humanity.  And it worked as the audience for that primary movie and any afterward is typically far more enamored with the new species of bugs and their role in combat compared to how the characters deal with those bugs).
So then, what is "Starship Troopers" primarily about?  Basically, it's a hit piece on how stupidly governments and militaries are run.  The whole book is a wide criticism of both modern government (anywhere in the world, including in the US) and how militaries are run (treating basically every soldier as stupid, expendible, and worth nothing).  That's what the book is exploring.  A fictional "government" and "military" that tries to "do things better".  Whether the audience agrees with those takes isn't really the point.  Exploring those takes is sort of the point of the book (though it basically only extolls the virtues of such systems, which is what basically every person does when they have an idea they think is great or will fix things).  The book proposes "You can eliminate all governmental stupidity and corruption by requiring anyone in office serve out a dangerous military term where they learn the value of protecting Humanity and putting Humanity before themselves, as well as only letting those people vote so that corruption can't be easily elected into office" and "we really shouldn't have any stupid soldiers and all soldiers should be trained to be highly capable and highly intelligent where the only difference in rank is how good their leadership skill actually is".  That's the book.
It is basically Johnny Rico editorializing everything he thinks is great about his current government and how the military actually works.  Johnny could've been replaced with anyone.  Book isn't about him.  The war exists in the book purely to show off how the military should work in practice, it could've been against anyone or anything (in practice, the bugs are basically the ultimate Communists, so they exist as both critique and virtue of that system as well).  So, the story or the characters don't matter at all.  It isn't an exploration of either of those things.  It's a book that explores a fictional "governmental utopia" and uses that utopia to leverage heavy criticism against all current governments and all current military training/doctrine.
Heck, if you want a story that also does something similar (with actual fascism, not just media implied fascism from people who didn't read the book), you could look at "Brave New World".  This is also a story about "The setting and premise".  The characters don't actually matter that much, only the system they interact with matters... and there's really no "story" in it at all.  The basic premise of the story is "this system exists, so what happens when you bring someone in from outside, who lives in the ghetto and was abused their whole lives, and has to interact with this system".  It's also a story about "an idea", rather than having an actual story or characters to care about.
Sci Fi stories generally engage in this "exploration of ideas" most often, but other genres do it as well.
It's all just a matter of "using the right tool for the job".
If you have a really interesting premise, then maybe your characters don't matter that much.
If you have really great characters, then maybe the story they're in really doesn't matter that much.
If you don't have a premise or characters you feel are interesting... then why not just write a "think piece" on your own worldview?  That works, too.
Or, in the case of video games:
It's possible that the point of the video game you're making is to play the video game, you know, like a board game.  You aren't playing Sorry! for character development or a rich storyline.  You're playing it because it's fun.
Video games can be "just for fun" too.  They don't necessarily need anything in them beyond the systems you employ.  Though... then you get into tricky territory of "is this actually an RPG, then?" without those things.  Which is a different discussion entirely.

What I found to work and accidentally makes my games better overall is to not have 'random' npcs, but make a character for each one. You don't need them to be super deep, but even a single characterization (This NPC recently moved into the city because they have a crush on the librarian) can help direct your thoughts on what NPC chatter is about. I find it often leads to adding mini-miniquests because you'll notice certain NPCs seem to have wants the player could (easily?) help with.
